title: Marathi Cinema's ₹130-Crore King Just Arrived on Netflix — and the Diaspora Finally Gets a Seat
excerpt: Riteish Deshmukh's Raja Shivaji, the most expensive and highest-grossing Marathi film of all time, is now streaming globally in Hindi and Marathi.
body:
The film that turned Marathi cinema into a blockbuster industry just walked into your living room.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=k6IQrT4egPI</youtube>

**Raja Shivaji**, Riteish Deshmukh's sweeping historical epic about the founding of the Maratha Empire, began streaming on **Netflix** on June 26 — and if you're part of the Indian diaspora and missed the theatrical run, this is the weekend to clear your schedule.

Let's talk scale. Riteish didn't just act in this one. He directed it, produced it alongside wife **Genelia Deshmukh** and **Jio Studios**, and assembled a cast that reads like a Bollywood roll call from a parallel timeline where everyone said yes at the same time. **Sanjay Dutt** plays Afzal Khan with the kind of menacing gravitas he was born for. **Abhishek Bachchan** shows up. **Vidya Balan** takes on Khadija Sultana. **Bhagyashree** is here. **Sachin Khedekar**, **Fardeen Khan**, **Jitendra Joshi**, **Boman Irani**, **Mahesh Manjrekar**, **Amol Gupte** — it keeps going. And then there's the cameo: **Salman Khan** as Jeeva Mahala, the warrior who defended Shivaji Maharaj during a pivotal battle, delivering action sequences that are already some of the most replayed clips from the film.

> This is not a small Marathi film that happened to do well. This is a ₹75-crore production — the most expensive Marathi film ever made — that crossed ₹100 crore at the Indian box office.

The numbers are staggering for the Marathi industry. Released on Maharashtra Day (May 1, 2026), **Raja Shivaji** ran for six unbroken weeks in theatres, accumulating ₹105.68 crore net domestically. Factor in a gross of ₹124.7 crore at home and ₹5 crore from overseas, and you get a worldwide total of ₹129.7 crore. For a Marathi-language film, that's not a record — it's a different category entirely. This is now the **highest-grossing Marathi film of all time**, and by a considerable margin.

What makes the film work is the discipline of its storytelling. Cinematographer **Santosh Sivan** — the man behind *Dil Se*, *Before the Rains*, and a dozen other visual masterpieces — shoots the Deccan and Maharashtra's fort country like it's a character in itself. The light hitting the ramparts of Raigad, the dust rising as Shivaji's soldiers move through narrow passes — Sivan makes history look tactile. The score by **Ajay-Atul** (of *Sairat* and *Drishyam* fame) swells exactly when it should and retreats into silence when the weight of the moment demands it.

The narrative covers Shivaji Maharaj's early life under the guidance of **Rajmata Jijabai**, through to his rallying of loyalists, the strategic capture of forts, and the iconic confrontation with Afzal Khan — the encounter that became the stuff of legend and folk ballad. Rather than reducing the story to a single battle or a single act of defiance, the film traces the architecture of rebellion: how guerrilla warfare, loyalty, and sheer tactical brilliance were used to challenge the Adil Shahi Sultanate and the Mughal Empire and lay the foundations of Swarajya, self-rule.

Riteish's performance in the title role has drawn both praise and honest debate. The criticism — primarily around some of the VFX work — hasn't aged the film; if anything, the rawness of certain sequences gives the whole thing a handmade quality that feels appropriate for a labour-of-love project of this ambition. This is a filmmaker who put himself on screen as one of India's most revered historical figures and then had to stand by every frame. Whether or not every visual effect lands, the commitment is unmistakable.

### Where to Watch

**Raja Shivaji** is streaming now on **Netflix** in both **Hindi** and **Marathi**. For the diaspora, that means global availability — US, UK, Canada, the Gulf, Singapore, wherever you are. No hunting for links, no waiting for a satellite premiere. Just open Netflix.

### What's Next for Riteish

This is barely a breath before the next one. Riteish is already deep into promotions for **Dhamaal 4**, the long-awaited comedy sequel arriving in theatres on July 10. Two weeks after Netflix gives the world his most serious work, cinemas will give them his most chaotic. That range? That's star power.

And if you're watching **Raja Shivaji** this weekend, pay attention to the quiet moments — the ones where Riteish lets Shivaji's eyes do the talking. They'll stay with you longer than any battle.
